lessons.title: Conservation of energy, power and efficiency
lessons.summary: Understand that energy is conserved but dissipates, calculate power and efficiency, and explain how insulation and lubrication reduce unwanted energy transfers.
objectives: I can state the law of conservation of energy and explain what dissipation means.
I can calculate power using $P = E/t$ and $P = W/t$.
I can calculate efficiency from useful and total energy or power and give it as a decimal or percentage.
I can explain how lubrication, insulation and thermal conductivity affect unwanted energy transfers.

activities.title: Energy is conserved
activities.content:
## The law of conservation of energy

> Energy can be **transferred** usefully, **stored** or **dissipated**, but it can never be **created or destroyed**.

The total energy in a **closed system** (one where nothing gets in or out) never changes. When a bouncing ball gradually stops, energy has not disappeared; it has spread out into the thermal stores of the ball, floor and air.

## Dissipation

In every real process, some energy ends up spread thinly across the surroundings, usually as a small temperature rise. This energy is **dissipated**. We often call it *wasted* because it is no longer useful, but it still exists. Common causes:

- **Friction** between moving parts warms them up.
- **Air resistance** warms the air around a moving object.
- **Electrical resistance** warms wires and components.
- **Sound** carries energy away from a machine.

In any energy story, the useful transfer plus the dissipated energy always adds up to the total energy put in.

activities.title: Worked example: tracking the energy
activities.content:
**An electric drill is supplied with 500 J of energy. It transfers 320 J to the kinetic store of the drill bit. What happens to the rest?**

Total in = useful out + dissipated

$500 = 320 + \text{dissipated}$

$\text{dissipated} = 180$ J

The 180 J is transferred by heating (the motor and bearings get warm) and by sound to the thermal store of the surroundings. None of the 500 J has been destroyed.

**A pendulum is pulled to one side and released. Explain, using stores, why each swing is slightly lower than the last.**

At the top of each swing, energy is in the gravitational potential store; at the bottom, in the kinetic store. On every swing, air resistance transfers a little energy to the thermal store of the air. Less energy returns to the gravitational store, so the swing height falls. Total energy, including the dissipated part, stays the same.

question.text: A toy car is pushed along a carpet and comes to a stop. What has happened to the kinetic energy it had?
question.hint: Energy cannot be destroyed, so it must have gone somewhere.
question.explanation: Friction between the wheels and carpet transfers the kinetic energy to the thermal stores of the car, carpet and air. It is dissipated, not destroyed.

options.text: It has been dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings
It has been destroyed by friction
It has been stored in the car's chemical store
It has been stored as friction
options.feedback: Friction is a force, not a store.

activities.title: Power
activities.content:
## Power: how fast energy is transferred

**Power** is the rate at which energy is transferred, or the rate at which work is done.

$$P = \frac{E}{t} \qquad P = \frac{W}{t}$$

- $P$ = power in **watts (W)**
- $E$ = energy transferred in **joules (J)**
- $W$ = work done in **joules (J)**
- $t$ = time in **seconds (s)**

One watt means **one joule every second**. A 2000 W kettle transfers 2000 J each second. Large powers are given in **kilowatts (kW)**: 1 kW = 1000 W.

Two motors could lift the same crate through the same height, transferring the same energy, but the one that does it in half the time has **twice the power**.

**Unit traps**
- Time must be in seconds: 5 minutes = 300 s.
- Energy in kJ must be converted to J (× 1000).
- Do not confuse **W** for watts with **W** for work done in the equation; the context makes it clear.

activities.title: Worked example: power of a lift
activities.content:
**A lift motor does 90 000 J of work raising the lift in 30 s. Calculate its power.**

$P = \frac{W}{t} = \frac{90\,000}{30} = 3000$ W = 3 kW

**A 1.2 kW heater runs for 5 minutes. How much energy does it transfer?**

1. Convert: 1.2 kW = 1200 W; 5 minutes = 300 s
2. Rearrange: $E = Pt = 1200 \times 300 = 360\,000$ J = 360 kJ

**Two students, A and B, each climb the same stairs. Both gain 3000 J of gravitational potential energy. A takes 6 s and B takes 10 s. Who is more powerful?**

$P_A = 3000 \div 6 = 500$ W, $P_B = 3000 \div 10 = 300$ W. Student A transfers the same energy faster, so A is more powerful.

question.text: A microwave oven transfers 84 000 J of energy in 2 minutes. Calculate its power in watts.
question.hint: Convert the time into seconds before dividing.

activities.title: Efficiency
activities.content:
## Efficiency

Efficiency tells you what fraction of the energy put into a device does the useful job:

$$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output energy transfer}}{\text{total input energy transfer}}$$

Because power is energy per second, the same idea works with power:

$$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful power output}}{\text{total power input}}$$

Efficiency has **no units**. Write it as a **decimal** (0.6) or a **percentage** (60%). It can **never be more than 1 (100%)**, because that would mean getting more energy out than you put in, which breaks conservation of energy.

| Device | Typical efficiency |
|---|---|
| Electric motor | 0.85–0.95 |
| LED lamp | about 0.9 |
| Filament lamp | about 0.05 |
| Petrol engine | 0.25–0.35 |

If you calculate an efficiency above 1, check whether you divided the wrong way round or mixed up useful and total.

**Higher tier:** you may be asked to describe ways of increasing efficiency, such as lubricating moving parts, streamlining to cut air resistance, or using low-resistance wiring.

activities.title: Worked example: efficiency of a motor
activities.content:
**A motor is supplied with 1500 J of energy and lifts a load, giving it 1200 J of gravitational potential energy. Find the efficiency.**

$\text{efficiency} = \frac{1200}{1500} = 0.8$ or **80%**

The remaining 300 J is dissipated by heating and sound.

**A television has an efficiency of 0.35 and an input power of 200 W. What useful power does it produce (as light and sound)?**

Rearrange: useful output = efficiency × total input = $0.35 \times 200 = 70$ W

**A kettle is 90% efficient and transfers 180 000 J usefully to the water. How much energy did it take from the mains?**

Rearrange: total input = useful output ÷ efficiency = $180\,000 \div 0.9 = 200\,000$ J

question.text: A filament lamp has an input power of 60 W and gives out 3 W of useful light. Calculate its efficiency as a percentage.
question.hint: Divide the useful output by the total input, then multiply by 100.

question.text: True or false: a well-designed machine can have an efficiency of 1.2 if it is very well lubricated.
question.hint: What would an efficiency greater than 1 mean for the energy in and out?
question.explanation: False. Efficiency can never exceed 1 (100%) because the useful output can never be greater than the total input; that would create energy from nothing.

options.text: True
False

activities.title: Reducing unwanted energy transfers
activities.content:
## Cutting down on dissipation

**Lubrication**: oil or grease between moving surfaces reduces friction, so less energy is transferred to thermal stores and more goes where you want it.

**Thermal insulation**: materials that are poor conductors (trapped air, foam, wool, fibreglass) slow the rate at which energy is transferred by heating.

## Thermal conductivity

The **thermal conductivity** of a material tells you how quickly energy is transferred through it by heating. Metals have high conductivity; air, plastics and wool have low conductivity.

For a building, the rate of cooling depends on:

- the **thermal conductivity** of the walls: lower conductivity means slower cooling;
- the **thickness** of the walls: thicker walls cool the building more slowly.

## Insulating a house

| Method | How it works |
|---|---|
| Cavity wall insulation | foam fills the gap between two brick layers, trapping air and reducing conduction and convection |
| Loft insulation | fibreglass traps air, reducing conduction through the ceiling |
| Double glazing | air or argon between panes has low conductivity |
| Draught excluders | reduce convection currents through gaps |

**Required practical idea**: fill identical beakers with hot water, wrap each in a different insulating material of the same thickness, and record the temperature every minute. The slowest fall in temperature shows the best insulator. Control the starting temperature, water volume and material thickness.

question.text: Which **two** changes would reduce the rate at which a house loses energy to the outside?
question.hint: Think about wall thickness and conductivity.
question.explanation: Thicker walls and lower thermal conductivity both slow the rate of energy transfer by heating. Thinner walls and higher conductivity would speed it up.

options.text: Making the walls thicker
Using a wall material with lower thermal conductivity
Replacing brick walls with thin metal panels
options.feedback: Metal has a high thermal conductivity and thin walls lose energy faster.

options.text: Removing the loft insulation

question.text:
An electric winch is used to lift a 120 kg crate through a height of 5 m in 8 s. The winch motor has an input power of 1250 W. Use $g$ = 9.8 N/kg.

(a) Calculate the useful work done on the crate. **(2 marks)**

(b) Calculate the useful power output of the winch. **(1 mark)**

(c) Calculate the efficiency of the winch and describe what happens to the energy that is not transferred usefully. **(2 marks)**
question.hint: Useful work is the gain in gravitational potential energy, $mgh$. Then divide by time to get power, and compare with the input power.
question.explanation: (a) $W = mgh = 120 \times 9.8 \times 5 = 5880$ J. (b) $P = 5880 \div 8 = 735$ W. (c) efficiency $= 735 \div 1250 = 0.588$, about 59%. The remaining energy is dissipated: friction in the gears and resistance in the motor windings transfer energy to the thermal store of the winch and surroundings, and some is carried away by sound.

markScheme.criterion: Wasted energy dissipated to thermal store of surroundings by friction / resistance / sound

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- Energy is **conserved**: it is transferred, stored or dissipated, never created or destroyed.
- **Dissipated** energy spreads into thermal stores of the surroundings and is no longer useful.
- **Power** $P = E/t = W/t$, measured in watts (1 W = 1 J/s). Time in seconds!
- **Efficiency** = useful output ÷ total input (energy or power). No units, never above 1.
- Reduce dissipation with **lubrication** (less friction) and **insulation** (low thermal conductivity, thick walls).

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the law of conservation of energy.

metadata.blanksText: Energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but it cannot be ___ or ___.

practiceQuestions.hint: Two opposite words: one about making, one about getting rid of.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; the total in a closed system is constant.

practiceQuestions.text: A 2.5 kW immersion heater runs for 20 minutes. Calculate the energy it transfers, in joules.
practiceQuestions.hint: 2.5 kW = 2500 W and 20 minutes = 1200 s. Use $E = Pt$.

practiceQuestions.text: A student of mass 50 kg runs up a flight of stairs 4 m high in 5 s. Calculate the student's useful power output. Use $g$ = 9.8 N/kg.
practiceQuestions.hint: Work done = $mgh$, then divide by the time.

practiceQuestions.text: An LED lamp has an efficiency of 0.85. If its useful light output is 8.5 W, what is its input power in watts?
practiceQuestions.hint: Rearrange: total input = useful output ÷ efficiency.

practiceQuestions.text: A petrol engine is supplied with 8000 J of energy from fuel and does 2400 J of useful work. What is its efficiency?

options.feedback: An efficiency over 1 is impossible: you divided the wrong way round.
That is the fraction wasted, not the efficiency.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each way of reducing unwanted energy transfer to the situation where it is used.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about whether the problem is friction, conduction or draughts.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Oil lubricates the moving parts of a bike chain. Fibreglass in a loft traps air to reduce conduction. Draught excluders block convection currents through gaps.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: a material with a high thermal conductivity is a good insulator.
practiceQuestions.hint: Conductivity describes how easily energy passes through by heating.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. High thermal conductivity means energy is transferred through the material quickly, so it is a poor insulator. Good insulators have low thermal conductivity.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: Put these lamps in order of efficiency, most efficient first. Lamp X: 10 W in, 1 W light out. Lamp Y: 20 W in, 8 W light out. Lamp Z: 5 W in, 4 W light out.
practiceQuestions.hint: Work out useful ÷ total for each lamp before comparing.
practiceQuestions.explanation: X = 0.1, Y = 0.4, Z = 0.8. So the order is Z, Y, X.

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why lubricating the bearings of a wind turbine increases the useful energy it transfers.
practiceQuestions.hint: What does friction do to the energy, and what does lubrication do to friction?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Friction in the bearings transfers some of the kinetic energy of the blades to a thermal store, which is dissipated. Lubrication reduces friction, so less energy is dissipated and more is transferred usefully to the generator.

markScheme.criterion: Lubrication reduces friction between the moving surfaces
Less energy dissipated / transferred to thermal store, so more is transferred usefully

practiceQuestions.text:
A student investigates insulation by wrapping three identical beakers of hot water in different materials and recording the temperature every 2 minutes for 20 minutes.

(a) State **two** variables that must be kept the same for a fair comparison. **(2 marks)**

(b) Beaker A, wrapped in foam, cooled from 80 °C to 62 °C. Beaker B, wrapped in aluminium foil, cooled from 80 °C to 48 °C. Explain which material is the better insulator. **(2 marks)**
practiceQuestions.hint: Fair test: what could change the cooling rate apart from the material? For (b), compare the temperature drops.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Starting temperature, volume of water, thickness of insulation, beaker size, room temperature (any two). (b) Foam is the better insulator because beaker A lost only 18 °C compared with 32 °C for B; foam has a lower thermal conductivity (it traps air), so energy is transferred to the surroundings more slowly.

markScheme.criterion: One control variable: starting temperature / volume of water / thickness of material / room temperature / beaker type
Foam is the better insulator because its temperature fell less (18 °C vs 32 °C)
Foam has lower thermal conductivity / traps air, so energy is transferred more slowly

practiceQuestions.text: A child on a playground swing stops pushing. Each swing gets a little smaller until the swing hangs still. What has happened to the energy the swing had?
practiceQuestions.hint: Energy is conserved, so the total amount has not changed. Think about air resistance and the pivot at the top of the chains.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Air resistance and friction at the pivot do work on the swing, transferring its kinetic and gravitational potential energy to the thermal stores of the air, the pivot and the chains. The energy is dissipated, not destroyed.

options.text: It has been dissipated to the thermal stores of the air and the pivot
It has been destroyed by air resistance
options.feedback: Energy can never be destroyed; it is transferred to less useful stores.

options.text: It has been stored as friction in the chains
options.feedback: Friction is a force, not an energy store.

options.text: It has been transferred to the child's chemical store

practiceQuestions.text: A hair dryer transfers 135 000 J of energy in 1.5 minutes. Calculate its power in watts.
practiceQuestions.hint: Power is energy transferred per second, so change 1.5 minutes into seconds first.

practiceQuestions.text: A petrol lawnmower engine has an input power of 2.5 kW. Its useful output power is 600 W. Calculate the efficiency of the engine as a percentage.
practiceQuestions.hint: Both powers must be in the same unit before you divide: 2.5 kW is 2500 W.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: an electric motor with an efficiency of 0.65 dissipates 35% of the energy supplied to it.
practiceQuestions.hint: Efficiency is the useful fraction of the input. What fraction is left over?
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. An efficiency of 0.65 means 65% of the input energy is transferred usefully. The other 35% is dissipated, mostly to the thermal store of the motor and surroundings.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: A hot drink is left in a cup on a desk. Which **two** changes would reduce the rate at which the drink loses energy to the surroundings?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about thickness, thermal conductivity and how much of the drink is exposed.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A lid stops energy being carried away from the surface, and a thick-walled foam cup has a much lower thermal conductivity than thin metal. A wide bowl increases the exposed surface area and a metal tray conducts energy away through the base, so both speed up the loss.

options.text: Put a lid on the cup
Swap the thin metal cup for a thick-walled foam cup
Pour the drink into a wide, shallow bowl
options.feedback: A larger exposed surface loses energy faster.

options.text: Stand the cup on a metal tray
options.feedback: Metal conducts energy away from the base quickly.

practiceQuestions.text:
A hoist on a building site raises a 180 kg pallet of bricks through a height of 3.5 m in 6 s. The hoist motor has an input power of 1400 W. Use $g$ = 9.8 N/kg.

(a) Calculate the useful work done on the pallet. **(2 marks)**

(b) Calculate the useful power output of the hoist. **(1 mark)**

(c) Calculate the efficiency of the hoist and describe what happens to the energy that is not transferred usefully. **(2 marks)**
practiceQuestions.hint: The useful work is the gain in gravitational potential energy, $mgh$. Divide by the time to get useful power, then compare with the input power.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) $W = mgh = 180 \times 9.8 \times 3.5 = 6174$ J. (b) $P = \frac{6174}{6} = 1029$ W. (c) Efficiency $= \frac{1029}{1400} = 0.735$, about 74%. The rest of the input energy is dissipated: friction in the pulleys and gears and resistance in the motor coils transfer energy to the thermal store of the hoist and the surroundings, and a little is carried away as sound.

markScheme.criterion: Wasted energy dissipated to thermal store of surroundings by friction / resistance / sound
